claim: Classical theories propose that the motor system forms a single specification of the sequence as a whole, leading to the coarticulation of the different elements.
source: Classical theories propose that the motor system forms a single specification of the sequence as a whole, leading to the coarticulation of the different elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established theories in the field, representing existing scientific knowledge.

claim: Recent neural recordings challenge the idea of single specification and suggest independent execution of each element specified separately.
source: In contrast, recent neural recordings challenge this idea and suggest independent execution of each element specified separately.
evidence: This claim references recent neural recording studies, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Separate or coarticulated sequences can result from the same task-dependent controller, without implying different representations in the brain.
source: Here, we show that separate or coarticulated sequences can result from the same task-dependent controller, without implying different representations in the brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by simulations and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Planning for multiple reaches simultaneously allows separate or coarticulated sequences depending on instructions about intermediate goals.
source: Simulations show that planning for multiple reaches simultaneously allows separate or coarticulated sequences depending on instructions about intermediate goals.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In co-articulated sequences, the second goal influenced long-latency stretch responses to external loads applied during the first reach.
source: Furthermore, in co-articulated sequences, the second goal influenced long-latency stretch responses to external loads applied during the first reach, demonstrating the involvement of the sensorimotor network supporting fast feedback control.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human participants.

claim: The trajectory of sub-movements in a sequence is affected by multiple future goals.
source: Behavioral data from various sensorimotor repertoires indicate that the trajectory of sub-movements in a sequence is affected by multiple future goals (Ariani and Diedrichsen, 2019; Diamond et al., 2017; Gottwald et al., 2018; Sheahan et al., 2016; Sosnik et al., 2004; Kashefi et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple behavioral studies.

claim: In human speech and bird song, the pronunciation of individual elements is influenced by subsequent elements, a phenomenon known as coarticulation.
source: For example, in human speech and bird song, the pronunciation of individual elements is influenced by subsequent elements (Fowler and Saltzman, 1993; Wohlgemuth et al., 2010), a phenomenon known as coarticulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on speech and bird song.

claim: Concatenating multiple sub-movements into larger units (chunks) induces coarticulation within the velocity patterns of sub-movements.
source: Ramkumar and colleagues (Ramkumar et al., 2016) employed a computational model, revealing that concatenating multiple sub-movements into larger units, referred to as chunks (Verwey, 2001; Verwey and Abrahamse, 2012), induces coarticulation within the velocity patterns of sub-movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a computational modeling study.

claim: Recent neural recordings in the primary motor cortex (M1) have shown no specific influence of future goals on the population responses governing ongoing action.
source: Recent neural recordings in the primary motor cortex (M1) have shown no specific influence of future goals on the population responses governing ongoing action (Yokoi and Diedrichsen, 2019; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neural recording studies.

claim: In a two-reach sequence task, there was no coarticulation in sub-movement kinematics although the execution got faster with practice.
source: Specifically, (Zimnik and Churchland, 2021) observed in a two-reach sequence task that, there was no coarticulation in sub-movement kinematics although the execution got faster with practice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: M1 displayed separate phases of execution-related activity for each sub-movement.
source: Notably, M1 displayed separate phases of execution-related activity for each sub-movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to neural recording data.

claim: Sequence goals could be separated and serially specified to the controller from regions upstream of M1.
source: Using a neural network model, they interpreted that sequence goals could be separated and serially specified to the controller from regions upstream of M1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation from a neural network model in a cited study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Earlier studies showed coarticulation of sub-movements and whole sequence representations in M1.
source: These findings contrast with earlier studies showing coarticulation of sub-movements and whole sequence representations in M1 (Ben-Shaul et al., 2004; Hatsopoulos et al., 2003; Lu and Ashe, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to earlier neural recording studies.

claim: Human motor control involves continuous processing of sensory feedback.
source: As a consequence, the role of feedback control in this debate has been unexplored, although it is known that human motor control involves continuous processing of sensory feedback (Crevecoeur and Kurtzer, 2018; Parrell and Houde, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on sensory feedback in motor control.

claim: The theory of optimal feedback control (OFC) has been useful in predicting the influence of numerous task parameters on the controller.
source: The theory of optimal feedback control (OFC) has been particularly useful in predicting the influence of numerous task parameters on the controller (Diedrichsen et al., 2010; Cluff and Scott, 2013; Cluff and Scott, 2015; Kalidindi and Crevecoeur, 2023; Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Scott, 2004; Kurtzer et al., 2008; De Comite et al., 2022), thus reproducing goal-directed motor commands during both unperturbed movements and feedback responses to disturbances (Kalidindi and Crevecoeur, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to OFC studies.

claim: OFC has been used to interpret flexible feedback responses occurring in the long-latency response period.
source: OFC has been used in numerous studies to interpret flexible feedback responses occurring in the long-latency response period (Kalidindi and Crevecoeur, 2023; Scott, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using OFC framework.

claim: In the OFC framework, all targets in a sequence can be considered simultaneously by the controller, and the overlap between control gains applied to each target determines when they influence the sequence.
source: In this framework, all targets in a sequence can be considered simultaneously by the controller, and the overlap between control gains applied to each target determines when they influence the sequence (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical prediction from the OFC framework, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Control gains depend on task requirements.
source: The control gains themselves depend on task requirements (Liu and Todorov, 2007; Dimitriou et al., 2013; Cesonis and Franklin, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on task-dependent control gains.

claim: Even if the sequence is considered as a whole at the level of controller, control gains can show different amounts of overlap based on task requirements, leading to either coarticulation or separation of the sequence elements.
source: OFC predicts two experimentally testable features of sequence production: first, even if the sequence is considered as a whole at the level of controller, control gains can show different amounts of overlap based on task requirements, leading to either coarticulation or separation of the sequence elements
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the OFC model presented in the study.

claim: In sequences with strong co-articulation, feedback responses to perturbations are expected to depend on future targets due to the overlap of control gains.
source: second, in sequences with strong co-articulation, feedback responses to perturbations are expected to depend on future targets due to the overlap of control gains.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the OFC model presented in the study.

claim: The instruction to slow-down at the first target influenced the coarticulation of the two reaches in simulations.
source: Simulations revealed that the instruction to slow-down at the first target influenced the coarticulation of the two reaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The penalty for the velocity at the first target produced an apparent separation of two reaches, even if the controller was always computed jointly for both reaches.
source: Importantly, the penalty for the velocity at the first target produced an apparent separation of two reaches, even if the controller was always computed jointly for both reaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human behavior was fully consistent with the simulations.
source: We conducted two experiments with human participants and observed that their behavior was fully consistent with the simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human participants.

claim: Flexible coarticulation dependent on task instruction about the intermediate target was observed in human experiments.
source: We observed both flexible coarticulation dependent on task instruction about the intermediate target, as well as a modulation of long-latency feedback responses to the mechanical loads applied during the first reach dependent on the location of the second target when coarticulation was present.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human participants.

claim: Long-latency feedback responses to mechanical loads applied during the first reach were modulated dependent on the location of the second target when coarticulation was present.
source: We observed both flexible coarticulation dependent on task instruction about the intermediate target, as well as a modulation of long-latency feedback responses to the mechanical loads applied during the first reach dependent on the location of the second target when coarticulation was present.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human participants.

claim: Recordings of muscle activity suggest that the operation of sequence production is carried out by the sensorimotor network that mediates fast state-feedback control.
source: Recordings of muscle activity suggest that this operation is carried out by the sensorimotor network that mediates fast state-feedback control.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from muscle activity recordings presented in the study.

claim: The model considers a task-dependent state-feedback controller derived from the framework of stochastic optimal control.
source: The model considers a task-dependent state-feedback controller derived from the framework of stochastic optimal control (Kalidindi and Crevecoeur, 2023).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: Feedback control gains are tuned to task demands and vary within a movement.
source: Importantly, feedback gains are tuned to task demands (Liu and Todorov, 2007; Nashed et al., 2012), and vary within a movement (Dimitriou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on feedback control gains.

claim: When there was no constraint on speed at the first target, the simulated hand reached the first target with a high velocity.
source: When there was no constraint on speed at the first target, the simulated hand reached the first target with a high velocity (Figure 2C, left panel), and subsequently continued towards the second target at a high initial speed of >0.2 m/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the rapid transfer scenario, the control gains showed a cross-over effect where the control gain associated with the second target (k2) was non-zero during the first reach.
source: In this rapid transfer scenario, the control gains showed a cross-over effect where the control gain associated with the second target (k2) was non-zero, albeit small, during the first reach, showing an early overlap with the feedback gain (k1) (Figure 2C, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The location of the second target influenced the lateral hand deviation of the first reach in the rapid transfer scenario.
source: As a result, the location of the second target influenced the lateral hand deviation of the first reach (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The trajectories following external loads applied to the mass were dependent on the second target in the rapid transfer scenario.
source: Because the control gains also determine the response to external perturbations, the trajectories following external loads applied to the mass were also dependent on the second target (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The lateral deviation along the perturbed direction was smaller when the second target was in the direction of perturbation.
source: Interestingly, the lateral deviation along the perturbed direction was smaller when the second target was in the direction of perturbation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: A smaller hand deviation is necessary to avoid high acceleration at T1 when the perturbation is in the direction of T2.
source: Although this may appear counterintuitive, the model shows that it is an efficient solution, because a higher acceleration linked to reversal at T1, when the perturbation is in the direction of T2, incurs a higher motor cost. Hence, a smaller hand deviation is necessary to avoid high acceleration at T1.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the model's optimization principles.

claim: The requirement to slow down at the first target reduced the velocity at the end of the first reach and altered the shape of the trajectories.
source: On the contrary, the requirement to slow down at the first target, captured by an increased cost on speed, reduced the velocity at the end of the first reach and altered the shape of the trajectories (Figure 2D, left panel) compared to the rapid transfer scenario (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The control gain corresponding to the second target became non-zero at a later time when there was a requirement to slow down at the first target.
source: The control gain corresponding to the second target became non-zero at a later time, at the end of the first reach (Figure 2D, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Due to the later increase in control gain, the influence of the second target on the motor output during the first reach was much reduced, generating a similar hand path to reach the first target across the two sequences.
source: Due to the later increase in this gain value, the influence of the second target on the motor output during the first reach was much reduced, hence generating a similar hand path to reach the first target across the two sequences (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Feedback responses to lateral perturbations applied early-on in the first reach were not dependent on the location of the second target when there was a requirement to slow down at the first target.
source: Similarly, feedback responses to lateral perturbations that were applied early-on in the first reach were not dependent on the location of the second target (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The hand did not come to rest at the end of the first reach in the rapid transfer scenario, but continued towards the second target at a relatively high transfer speed of ~0.2 m/s.
source: Figure 3A illustrates the average hand speed across baseline trials in the rapid transfer scenario. It is clear that the hand did not come to rest at the end of the first reach, but continued towards the second target at a relatively high transfer speed of ~0.2 m/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The hand speed at the first target was slightly different between the 2 second target conditions (paired t-test: t(14) = –3.8, p=0.002).
source: The hand speed at the first target was slightly different between the 2 s target conditions (Figure 3A, inset; paired t-test: t(14) = –3.8, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the rapid transfer scenario, the location of the second target influenced the hand path during the first reach.
source: In line with model predictions, in the rapid transfer scenario, the location of the second target influenced the hand path during the first reach (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lateral hand deviation during the first reach was significantly different between the two sequences (paired t-test: t(14) = –5.9, p<10–4).
source: Statistically, across trials and participants, lateral hand deviation during the first reach was significantly different between the two sequences (Figure 3B, inset; paired t-test: t(14) = –5.9, p<10–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The hand deviation was significantly different between the leftward and rightward sequence conditions from the very first trial within a block (paired t-test: t(14) = 5.7, p<10–3).
source: Group data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 illustrate that the hand deviation was significantly different between the leftward and rightward sequence conditions from the very first trial within a block (paired t-test: t(14) = 5.7, p<10–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In rightward perturbation trials, the dwell velocity and hand deviation were significantly different across the 2 second target conditions (paired t-test: t(14) = –7.1, p<10–5 for dwell velocity; t(14) = –7.9, p<10–5 for hand deviation).
source: In rightward perturbation trials, the dwell velocity and hand deviation (Figure 3C and D) were significantly different across the 2 s target conditions (paired t-test: t(14) = –7.1, p<10–5 for dwell velocity; t(14) = –7.9, p<10–5 for hand deviation).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: Similar differences across the two sequences were observed in the leftward perturbation trials (paired t-test: t(14) = 6.9, p<10–5 for dwell velocity; t(14) = –8.2, p<10–6 for hand deviation).
source: Similar differences across the two sequences were observed in the leftward perturbation trials (Figure 3E and F) (paired t-test: t(14) = 6.9, p<10–5 for dwell velocity; t(14) = –8.2, p<10–6 for hand deviation).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: Lateral hand deviation was smaller when the perturbation was in the direction of the second target (T2) and vice-versa.
source: The influence of the second target on the lateral hand deviation was qualitatively similar to that observed in model simulations, and counterintuitive to what we might expect without the help of the model simulations. As observed in the model simulations (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2), lateral hand deviation was smaller when the perturbation was in the direction of the second target (T2) and vice-versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with model simulations.

claim: Both PEC and PD muscles displayed a clear difference in baseline EMG activity during the first reach, depending on whether the following reach involved right or left second targets.
source: Notably, both muscles displayed a clear difference in baseline EMG activity during the first reach, depending on whether the following reach involved right or left second targets (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The perturbation response in the stretched muscle was visibly larger if the second reach involved movement reversal compared to the first reach where the perturbation was in the direction of the second target.
source: The perturbation response in the stretched muscle – PEC for the rightward load (Figure 3H, left panel) and PD muscle for the leftward load (Figure 3I, right panel) – was visibly larger if the second reach involved movement reversal compared to the first reach where the perturbation was in the direction of the second target.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: The unloading response in the unstretched (shortened) muscle was larger if the second reach involved direction reversal.
source: Interestingly, even the unloading response (below baseline) in the unstretched (shortened) muscle – PD for the rightward load (Figure 3H, right panel) and PEC for the leftward load (Figure 3I, left panel) – was larger if the second reach involved direction reversal.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: When perturbed in the rightward direction, the PEC muscle stretch response was significantly larger in the rightward sequence than the leftward sequence in the long-latency epoch, in both R2 (one tail paired t-test: t(14) = 3.5, P<0.002) and R3 (one tail paired t-test: t(14) = 2.25, P=0.02).
source: Indeed the PEC stretch response was significantly larger in the rightward sequence than the leftward sequence in the long-latency epoch, in both R2 (one tail paired t-test: t(14) = 3.5, P<0.002) and R3 (one tail paired t-test: t(14) = 2.25, P=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: The PD muscle shortening response was significantly larger (below baseline) in the rightward sequence than the leftward sequence in both R2 (one-tailed paired t-test: t(14) = –3.2, P=0.003) and R3 epochs (one-tailed paired t-test: t(14) = –3.5, P=0.002).
source: On the other hand, the PD muscle shortening response was significantly larger (below baseline) in the rightward sequence than the leftward sequence in both R2 (one-tailed paired t-test: t(14) = –3.2, P=0.003) and R3 epochs (one-tailed paired t-test: t(14) = –3.5, P=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: When the perturbation load was to the left, the PEC shortening response was significantly larger in the leftward sequence compared to the rightward sequence in both R2 (one tail t-test: t(14) = 7, P<10–5) and R3 epochs (t(14) = 8.1, P<10–6).
source: When the perturbation load was to the left, the PEC shortening response (below baseline) was significantly larger in the leftward sequence compared to the rightward sequence in both R2 (one tail t-test: t(14) = 7, P<10–5) and R3 epochs (t(14) = 8.1, P<10–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: The stretch response in PD muscle was not significantly larger in the leftward sequence throughout the long-latency time period (one-tail paired t-test; R2 epoch: t(14) = 2.8, P=0.99; R3 epoch: t(14) = –0.13, P=0.44).
source: While the shortening response in PEC was larger, the stretch response in PD muscle was not significantly larger in the leftward sequence throughout the long-latency time period (one-tail paired t-test; R2 epoch: t(14) = 2.8, P=0.99; R3 epoch: t(14) = –0.13, P=0.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: All muscles exhibited differences in the voluntary time window (120–180ms) during the first reach depending on the location of the second target (two-tailed paired t-test: t (14) absolute value between (3.5–7.4), and p-value between (1e–6 – 0.012) across muscles and perturbation types).
source: All muscles exhibited differences in the voluntary time window (120–180ms) during the first reach depending on the location of the second target (two-tailed paired t-test: t (14) absolute value between (3.5–7.4), and p-value between (1e–6 – 0.012) across muscles and perturbation types).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: No sequence-related modulation of the stretch responses in the R1 epoch was observed, suggesting that potential differences at baseline did not have a strong impact.
source: We did not observe any sequence-related modulation of the stretch responses in the R1 epoch, suggesting that any potential differences at baseline did not have a strong impact.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of EMG data in the R1 epoch.

claim: When required to perform movement sequences rapidly, the sensorimotor circuits that mediate long latency feedback responses showed modulation that was dependent on the secondary target.
source: Overall, the results indicate, the when required to perform movement sequences rapidly, the sensorimotor circuits that mediate long latency feedback responses showed modulation that was dependent on the secondary target.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results.

claim: The hand speed at the first target dropped to near zero levels in all unperturbed, leftward, and rightward perturb conditions in the STOP task.
source: Figure 5 illustrates that the hand speed at the first target dropped to near zero levels in all unperturbed, leftward, and rightward perturb conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no influence of the second target on the velocity of reaching the first target in the STOP task (two-tailed paired t-test: t(13) = –1.9, P=0.08 in the baseline condition; t(13) = –0.01, P=0.99 for rightward perturbations; t(13) = 2.1, P=0.055 for leftward perturbations).
source: Clearly, there was no influence of the second target on the velocity of reaching the first target (two-tailed paired t-test: t(13) = –1.9, P=0.08 in the baseline condition; t(13) = –0.01, P=0.99 for rightward perturbations; t(13) = 2.1, P=0.055 for leftward perturbations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The hand deviation during the first reach was similar between the two sequences in the STOP task (two-tailed paired t-test: t(13) = –1.8, P=0.08 in the baseline condition; t(13) = –1.2, P=0.26 for rightward perturbations; t(13) = –1.2, P=0.25 for leftward perturbations).
source: The hand deviation during the first reach was similar between the two sequences (two-tailed paired t-test: t(13) = –1.8, P=0.08 in the baseline condition; t(13) = –1.2, P=0.26 for rightward perturbations; t(13) = –1.2, P=0.25 for leftward perturbations).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The unperturbed EMG responses of the PEC and PD muscles were similar throughout the first reach in the STOP task, and diverged only after the end of the first reach, while moving toward the second targets (T2).
source: Moreover, the unperturbed EMG responses of the PEC and PD muscles were similar throughout the first reach, and diverged only after the end of the first reach, while moving toward the second targets (T2).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data from the STOP task.

claim: In rightward and leftward perturbation conditions in the STOP task, the perturbation responses (ΔEMG) of the PEC and PD muscles were not statistically different in pre-perturbation, R1, R2, or R3 epochs.
source: In rightward and leftward perturbation conditions, the perturbation responses (ΔEMG) of the PEC and PD muscles (Figure 5D and E, and Figure 6) were not statistically different in pre-perturbation, R1, R2, or R3 epochs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The second target did not influence the first reach when the hand was required to slow-down at the first target.
source: To conclude, these results suggested that the second target did not influence the first reach when the hand was required to slow-down at the first target.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results from the STOP task.

claim: Both apparent separation or coarticulation of the two motor patterns can be explained within the same framework of flexible feedback control.
source: While this is conceptually valid, it is not necessary and the model provides a more nuanced view: both apparent separation or coarticulation of the two motor patterns can be explained within the same framework of flexible feedback control.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the model and experimental results.

claim: The results are consistent with recent behavioral studies showing that the information about future targets in a sequential task is integrated at the stage of motor planning.
source: The results presented here are consistent with recent behavioral studies showing that the information about future targets in a sequential task is integrated at the stage of motor planning (Diamond et al., 2017; Gottwald et al., 2018; Kashefi et al., 2024; Ariani et al., 2021; Engel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited behavioral studies.

claim: The coarticulation and separation of sequence components depended on task instructions, and likely reflected efficient solutions of the same continuous control problem with distinct penalties at the intermediate goals.
source: Our key contribution is twofold: we showed from computational and behavioral perspectives that the coarticulation and separation of sequence components depended on task instructions, and likely reflected efficient solutions of the same continuous control problem with distinct penalties at the intermediate goals
evidence: This is a summary of the study's key findings.

claim: Long-latency feedback control was modulated by future targets in a coarticulated sequence, consistent with theories suggesting that movement planning is synonymous with derivation of a control policy.
source: second, the results highlighted that long-latency feedback control was modulated by future targets in a coarticulated sequence, consistent with theories suggesting that movement planning is synonymous with derivation of a control policy (Crevecoeur et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's key findings with citation support.

claim: An artificial neural network model with simultaneous processing of targets reproduced the population activity of the primary motor cortex.
source: Consistent with this model (Figure 1B), recently an artificial neural network model with simultaneous processing of targets reproduced the population activity of the primary motor cortex (see Wang et al., 2024), a region that contributes significantly to long latency feedback responses (Scott, 2016; Pruszynski et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent neural network modeling study.

claim: The primary motor cortex contributes significantly to long latency feedback responses.
source: Consistent with this model (Figure 1B), recently an artificial neural network model with simultaneous processing of targets reproduced the population activity of the primary motor cortex (see Wang et al., 2024), a region that contributes significantly to long latency feedback responses (Scott, 2016; Pruszynski et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on M1 and feedback responses.

claim: In the framework of optimal feedback control, an intermediate goal is equivalent to a via-point that constrains the execution of the sequence.
source: Notably, in the framework of optimal feedback control, an intermediate goal is equivalent to a via-point that constrains the execution of the sequence (similar to Ramkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical interpretation with citation support.

claim: Coarticulation in motor systems may be processed similarly as other kinds of movement constraints, such as via-points, avoiding obstacles, or changes in control policies.
source: It is thus possible that coarticulation in motor systems be processed similarly as other kinds of movement constraints, such as via-points, avoiding obstacles, or changes in control policies.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The preparatory activity may not discern independently planned or coarticulated sequences because these situations imply different control policies (and cost functions), as opposed to different initial states.
source: A corollary of this definition is that the preparatory activity (Zimnik and Churchland, 2021; Ames et al., 2019) may not discern independently planned or coarticulated sequences because these situations imply different control policies (and cost functions), as opposed to different initial states.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the OFC framework with citation support.

claim: The nature of the sequence representation is potentially not dissociable from its execution.
source: Moreover, the nature of the sequence representation is potentially not dissociable from its execution for the same reason.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the OFC framework.

claim: Motor chunking may represent the formation of a composite cost function, hence a composite control policy, that can jointly optimize multiple sub-movements.
source: From our model, motor chunking (or a unified representation) does not necessarily imply a single (unified) preparatory period signal representing multiple goals. Motor chunking may represent the formation of a composite cost function, hence a composite control policy, that can jointly optimize multiple sub-movements (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the OFC framework.

claim: Motor chunking results from an acquired motor ability to form overlapping control policies for contiguous sequence elements.
source: In this view, motor chunking results from an acquired motor ability to form overlapping control policies for contiguous sequence elements (Figure 1B and Figure 2).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the OFC framework.

claim: Even a motor chunk may falsely appear to be independently controlled, masking the signature of sequence representation in neural data even if the controller was formed at once by considering multiple goals.
source: Importantly this property depends on the instruction at intermediate goals, thus even a motor chunk may falsely appear to be independently controlled (Figure 1A), masking the signature of sequence representation in neural data even if the controller was formed at once by considering multiple goals.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the OFC framework.

claim: The potential impact of non-linear mechanics on limb trajectory could be completely suppressed by participants in Experiment 2.
source: However, the potential impact of non-linear mechanics on limb trajectory could be completely suppressed by participants in Experiment 2, since we observed a straight reach path, thus making the curvature observed in Experiment 1 more likely related to the task constraints rather than the biomechanics which did not differ between experiments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Biomechanical factors can influence coarticulation in a speech production task.
source: Yet, the quantification of how biomechanical factors influence control may deserve a dedicated work, as it has been shown that biomechanics can also influence coarticulation in a speech production task (Ostry et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on speech production.

claim: The simple linearized OFC models were crucial in determining the relationship between three properties of the task demands, its impact on coarticulation, and feedback control.
source: Despite the limitations, the simple linearized OFC models were crucial in determining the relationship between three properties of the task demands, its impact on coarticulation, and feedback control.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the utility of the model.

claim: The main feature of the model – to generate a task-dependent motor output as a combination of state feedback – is not limited to linear controllers and linear body dynamics, but is applicable even when the control policy is non-linear.
source: Furthermore, the main feature of the model – to generate a task-dependent motor output as a combination of state feedback – is not limited to linear controllers and linear body dynamics, but is applicable even when the control policy is non-linear (see Kalidindi et al., 2021; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on non-linear control.

claim: The modeling and empirical results describe the computations underlying a two-reaches sequence.
source: The modeling and empirical results presented here describe the computations underlying a two-reaches sequence.
evidence: This is a summary of the scope of the study.

claim: Longer sequences are expected to be formed in a similar way as there is no theoretical constraint on the number of intermediate goals in the model.
source: We expect that longer sequences be formed in a similar way as we showed that there is no theoretical constraint on the number of intermediate goals in the model and the addition of sequence elements is straightforward.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the model's theoretical properties.

claim: Swift execution of sequences was achieved by habituation, where a set of sequences are practiced for several days to months.
source: Besides the implication of our computational model of co-articulation, it has been often documented that swift execution of sequences was achieved by habituation, where a set of sequences are practiced for several days to months (Ramkumar et al., 2016; Yokoi and Diedrichsen, 2019; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021; Lu and Ashe, 2005; Berlot et al., 2020; Huberdeau et al., 2023; Ariani and Diedrichsen, 2019; Maceira-Elvira et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on motor learning.

claim: Participants received explicit information about the dwell constraints at the intermediate goal, resulting in quick coarticulation.
source: Here, the participants received explicit information about the dwell constraints at the intermediate goal, resulting in quick coarticulation (also see Sosnik et al., 2004; Kashefi et al., 2024; Friedman and Korman, 2019; Sosnik et al., 2007; Sporn et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental protocol with citation support.

claim: Task-dependent modulation of existing reaching controllers can be rapidly switched from one trial to another.
source: This is in line with task-dependent modulation of existing reaching controllers, which can be rapidly switched from one trial to another (De Comite et al., 2022; Cesonis and Franklin, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on task-dependent control.

claim: There exist several mechanisms operating at different time-scales and responsible for a combination of sequence elements.
source: This suggests that there exist several mechanisms operating at different time-scales and responsible for a combination of sequence elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of different learning mechanisms.

claim: One mechanism is a slow habituation process in which the subject learns de novo to build a novel controller for different elements in the sequence.
source: One mechanism is a slow habituation process in which the subject learns de novo to build a novel controller for different elements in the sequence (Huberdeau et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2021), whereas the other mechanism is a fast modulation of this consolidated controller by task demands.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on motor learning.

claim: The two mechanisms (slow habituation and fast modulation) are dissociable with perturbations.
source: In principle, the two mechanisms are dissociable with perturbations, which may allow future studies to investigate how they interact and to identify which brain regions mediate these components of skilled motor behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: A total of 29 volunteers (11 men, 18 women, aged between 20 and 35 years) participated in two experiments.
source: A total of 29 volunteers (11 men, 18 women, aged between 20 and 35 years) participated in two experiments (n=15 with 9 women in Experiment 1; and n=14 with 9 women in Experiment 2).
evidence: This describes the participant demographics in the study.

claim: All participants were neurologically healthy, and right-handed.
source: All participants were neurologically healthy, and right-handed and gave their informed consent according to a protocol approved by the ethics board at UCLouvain.
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics in the study.

claim: The experiments used a robotic device (endpoint KINARM, BKIN Technologies), permitting hand movement in the horizontal plane.
source: The experiments used a robotic device (endpoint KINARM, BKIN Technologies), permitting hand movement in the horizontal plane.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: The KINARM can perturb the arm by applying mechanical loads at the handle.
source: In addition to recording the hand kinematics and forces on the robot handle, the KINARM can perturb the arm by applying mechanical loads at the handle.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The first target was situated 18 cm in the forward direction on the midline, while the second target was either situated to the left or right from the midline, displaced laterally from the first target by 8 cm.
source: The first target was situated 18 cm in the forward direction on the midline, while the second target was either situated to the left or right from the midline, displaced laterally from the first target by 8 cm (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the spatial arrangement of targets in the experiment.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants were instructed to initiate the sequence as soon as they received the GO cues.
source: Participants (n=15) were instructed to initiate the sequence as soon as they received the GO cues.
evidence: This describes the experimental instructions.

claim: The first reach was deemed successful if T1 was reached between 500–650 ms after receiving the GO cue.
source: The first reach was deemed successful if T1 was reached between 500–650 ms after receiving the GO cue.
evidence: This describes the experimental criteria for success.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants were required to slow-down while reaching the first target (T1).
source: Participants (n=14) performed two-target reaching sequences similar to Experiment 1 except that they were required to slow-down while reaching the first target (T1).
evidence: This describes the key difference in instructions for Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the condition for the target T2 to turn red was that the hand velocity had to fall below a threshold of 0.5 cm/s.
source: In this experiment, the condition for the target T2 to turn red, indicating the participant to move towards it, was that the hand velocity had to fall below a threshold of 0.5 cm/s.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for Experiment 2.

claim: The experiments consisted of nine sets, where each set was composed of 10 blocks equally divided between rightward and leftward sequences.
source: The experiments consisted of nine sets, where each set was composed of 10 blocks equally divided between rightward and leftward sequences (i.e. five blocks with rightward and five blocks with leftward second target location relative to T1) (see Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A total of 900 trials were performed across nine sets.
source: Hence, a total of 900 trials were performed across nine sets (9 sets ×10 blocks/set × 10 trials/block = 900 trials).
evidence: This describes the total number of trials in the experiment.

claim: The activity of mono-articular shoulder muscles (pectorialis major and posterior deltoid) was recorded using Delsys Bagnoli surface EMG setup.
source: We recorded the activity of mono-articular shoulder muscles using Delsys Bagnoli surface EMG setup: pectorialis major (PEC) and posterior deltoid (PD), involved in the production of lateral forces and known to be largely recruited following similar perturbations with the same setup (Crevecoeur et al., 2020a; Mathew et al., 2020; De Comite et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the EMG recording methodology.

claim: The model describes the translation of a point-mass similar to the mass of an arm (m=2.5 kg) in the horizontal plane.
source: The model describes the translation of a point-mass similar to the mass of an arm (m=2.5 kg) in the horizontal plane.
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.
